newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE -- Flatter on jobs data, Fed fears.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE -- Flatter on jobs data, Fed fears.

text.p: It took the better part of the past two weeks for the U.S. Treasury market to nearly price out a Federal Reserve rate hike in July.
But a mostly strong tone to Friday's May employment report put a stop to that. A look at the yield curve now shows the market starting to put the Fed back into the equation.
"The market has become a bit more cautionary and its ability for to continue the recent rally is circumscribed," said William Sullivan, head of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Following the Friday morning report, the two-year note rose to 6.25 percent, while the 30-year bond was up to 6.90 percent -- from Thursay closing levels of 6.20 and 6.88 percent, respectively.

As a result, the spread between the two issues narrowed three basis points to 65 basis points, its lowest since May 19 -- the day before the Fed last met and left rates steady. By late Friday afternoon the spread stood at 67, with the two-year at 6.13 percent and the 30-year at 6.80 percent.

The spread had been as wide as 76 basis points as late as last Tuesday, when the market figured the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in July were rather low. Some players were saying the two-year note could fall to about 6.10 percent and the bond to 6.75 percent if the employment report came in weak.

Enter Friday's employment report. Non-farm payrolls were bullish for the market, rising a weaker-than-expected 138,000. But the civilian jobless rate dipped 0.1 percentage point to 4.8 percent, a bearish factor.
"There was something in the report for everybody," said Kevin Sluder, head trader at First Chicago Capital Markets.

Treasuries took about 10 minutes to digest the data. During that time, prices went down, back up, back down, back up, before staying lower for most of the morning. The short-end got hit the hardest, as the market bears won out.
Treasuries turned sharply higher just before midday, mainly on technical factors. Players noted the market's reversal did not change the view that the Fed may need to raise rates.

"Put the report all together and it makes a case that we need to be more concerned about the Fed moving in July than before," said Sluder, who predicts a rate hike next month. "This makes the trend to higher yields for the time being."
Not to mention a flatter yield curve.
"We could get a lot flatter," Sluder said. "But not right away. We may be hard pressed to get through 60 basis points."

That could mean just another seven basis points of flattening is still in the cards. Players said that scenario would likely come in the form of the two-year note rising to 6.40 percent and the bond to 7.00 percent, as the market looks to a 5.75 percent fed funds rate.
Analysts said that the bond will probably not go much above 7.00 percent due to strong demand, and the belief another rate hike would help keep inflation low.

"We do not have a sign of recalibration of attitudes because it is only one month's data," Sullivan said. "But the message (from the employment report) is so clear, so certain that it reintroduces the notion of Fed restraint in the future.

"The market recognizes that the hope there would be a sustained period of policy stability has been eliminated," he added, noting that if the Fed does not move in July, then it most likely will do so by the third quarter.
So, in the meantime, the short end will lead the market, given that it is more sensitive to Fed movements, thereby leaving the long bond in a tight 6-7/8 to 7 percent range.
"It's unpleasant to think about, but it could be happening," Sluder said. "Everything is well behaved. Inflation is well behaved and growth is solid but looks like it could be moderating.
"So you can't make a case that (bond) rates need to be a lot higher," he added. "But at the same time, you can't make a case rates need to be a lot lower."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
